messages.author: 71bfb5f1e96782a8
messages.subject: anova of unidimensional and twodimensional model fails under wlsmv
parts:
Hi,

i want to compare a uni- and a twodimensional model, but the anova fails, because the parameters are named different between the models

Error in .test_compute_partable_A_diff(m1 = m1, m0 = m0) : 
  lavaan ERROR: parameter in H1 not found in H0: visual =~ x1 (group =  1 )

Of course, since the factors have different names. the parameters have different names too. however, it works with the ML estimator and i ran similar analysis earlier, so this might be a bug?

thanks for looking into this, here is a minimal example:


HS.model <- '
    visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
    textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9
'
HS.model_2 <- '
    uni  =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5 + x6 + x7 + x8 + x9
'


fit1 <- cfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, estimator = "WLSMV")
fit2 <- cfa(HS.model_2, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, estimator = "WLSMV")

anova(fit1, fit2)

best, hans

messages.subject: RE: anova of unidimensional and twodimensional model fails under wlsmv
parts:
The first model has three common factors (or dimensions), not 2.  If you standardize the factors, you can reduce the dimensionality by forcing covariances to 1.  That will make the nesting clear.

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: anova of unidimensional and twodimensional model fails under wlsmv
parts:
On 05/08/2015 09:52 PM, Dr. Hans Hansen wrote:
> Hi,
>
> i want to compare a uni- and a twodimensional model, but the anova
> fails, because the parameters are named different between the models

When the estimator = WLSMV, the anova() function (which just calls the
lavTestLRT() function) uses (in 0.5-18) a method that requires clear
nesting at the parameter level between the various models.

So, you may try to find an alternative parameterization (as suggested by
Ed Ridgon) to make sure that the models are clearly nested.

Estimator ML uses another method, that only requires nesting at the
covariance/mean level.

Yves.

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: anova of unidimensional and twodimensional model fails under wlsmv
parts:
Are chi-square difference/likelihood ratio tests considered valid for pairs of models that differ in dimensionality? I was under the impression that models with reduced dimensionality in terms of the variables (as distinct from dimensionality in terms of parameters) constitute boundary solutions that can impact the validity of such statistics for model comparison. However, I just spent some time searching for literature and did not come up with anything that directly addressed this issue in SEM. Hayashi, Bentler & Yuan discuss the issue in relation to EFA. Others may be aware of literature that I did not find.

Hayashi, K., Benter, P. M. & Yuan, K.-H. (2007) On the Likelihood Ratio Test for the Number of Factors in Exploratory Factor Analysis. Structural Equation Modeling, 14, 505-526. DOI: 10.1080/10705510701301891

Thanks,
Keith

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: anova of unidimensional and twodimensional model fails under wlsmv
parts:
On 05/10/2015 06:58 PM, kmarkus via lavaan wrote:
> Are chi-square difference/likelihood ratio tests considered valid for
> pairs of models that differ in dimensionality? I was under the
> impression that models with reduced dimensionality in terms of the
> variables (as distinct from dimensionality in terms of parameters)
> constitute boundary solutions that can impact the validity of such
> statistics for model comparison.

It is often possible to reparameterize a one-dimensional model as a
two-dimensional model by adding all sorts of constraints. If this is
possible, the one-dimensional model is nested within the two-dimensional
model. Not in the strict 'parameter' sense, but in the more general
covariance/mean structure sense. See also

Bentler, P. M., & Satorra, A. (2010). Testing model nesting and
equivalence. _Psychological Methods, 15_, 111-123. doi:10.1037/a0019625

In this case (ie, models are nested in the general covariance/mean
structure sense), the regular chi-square difference test is still valid.

This is also true for the *scaled* chi-square difference test if you use
either the method described in Satorra & Bentler (2001), or the method
described in Satorra & Bentler (2010), but NOT if you use the method
described in Satorra (2000). The latter requires that the models are
nested in the strict parameter sense.

Satorra, A. (2000). Scaled and adjusted restricted tests in
multi-sample analysis of moment structures. In Heijmans, R.D.H.,
Pollock, D.S.G. & Satorra, A. (eds.), Innovations in multivariate
statistical analysis. A Festschrift for Heinz Neudecker
(pp.233-247). London: Kluwer Academic Publishers.

Satorra, A., & Bentler, P. M. (2001). A scaled difference
chi-square test statistic for moment structure analysis.
Psychometrika, 66(4), 507-514.

Satorra, A., & Bentler, P. M. (2010). Ensuring postiveness of the
scaled difference chi-square test statistic. Psychometrika, 75(2),
243-248.

Yves.

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: anova of unidimensional and twodimensional model fails under wlsmv
parts:
On 05/09/2015 10:58 PM, Dr. Hans Hansen wrote:
> works great. nonetheless, could you explain why this wasn't necessary in
> older lavaan versions?

In older lavaan versions (< 0.5-18), the default method for the scaled
difference test was method = "satorra.bentler.2001" (which requires no
parameter nesting). In lavaan 0.5-18, I changed this to method =
"satorra.2000", which (as you discovered) does need parameter nesting.

Yves.

Yves,
Thanks for the detailed response. Oddly, I was familiar with most of the papers you cited, but did not connect them to settling this issue. Somehow, I was under the impression that boundary solutions were an exception to the rule.

For those following the thread, it may be of interest to note that the distinction between covariance matrix nesting and parameter nesting goes back at least to Bentler and Bonett (1980, p. 592).

Keith
